lines.cap: **Narrator:** This is Kavya. She is twelve. In the school band, she plays the **triangle**.
**Kavya:** Forty-six bars of nothing. Then one ding. Bar forty-seven. That's my whole job.
**Narrator:** Band practice. Thirty-four degrees. The ceiling fans are doing their best.
**Narrator:** But this documentary isn't about Kavya. It's about the air between her triangle and your ears.
**Narrator:** Trillions of tiny air particles. This is one of them.
**Nigel:** Hi. Nigel. **Nitrogen** molecule. Air particle.
**Nigel:** Seventy-eight percent of the air is nitrogen. And everyone only talks about oxygen.
**Nigel:** I work in sound. Deliveries. Every drum, every ding, every 'Kavya, focus!'
**Nigel:** People think I carry sound to your ear. I don't go anywhere. I **pass it on**.
**Echo:** ...pass it on.
**Nigel:** That's Echo. The back wall. She doesn't talk. She just repeats things.
**Echo:** ...repeats things.
**Narrator:** Pass It On. Episode eleven: Bar Forty-Seven.
**Narrator:** Every sound starts with something **vibrating**: moving quickly **back and forth** about a fixed position.
**Nigel:** The drum. Hit it, and the drum **skin** vibrates.
**Nigel:** The guitar. Pluck it, and the **string** vibrates.
**Nigel:** The loudspeaker. Its **cone** vibrates in and out, shoving us. Rude.
**Kavya:** Mmmmmm.
**Nigel:** Kavya's **vocal cords**. Two flaps of tissue in her throat. They vibrate when she talks, sings or complains.
**Kavya:** Mostly complains.
**Archie:** Hi hi hi! Archie! **Argon**! One percent of the air! It's my first day!
**Nigel:** Archie's a trainee. Argon's a noble gas. Chemically, he reacts to nothing. Emotionally, to everything.
**Nigel:** Proof? Kavya, ding the triangle. Then grab it.
**Narrator:** She strikes it, then grips it. The sound **stops** at once.
**Nigel:** Stop the vibration, stop the sound. **Vibration is the source of all sound**. And sound is a form of **energy**.
**Kavya:** Can I do that again? That's more dinging than I get in the actual song.

chapters.title: Pass it on (but don't go anywhere)

lines.cap: **Narrator:** So how does one ding cross the hall?
**Archie:** Easy! I grab the sound and RUN it over there!
**Nigel:** No.
**Nigel:** The triangle knocks the particles next to it. They bump their neighbours, who bump theirs. All the way across.
**Nigel:** Each of us just vibrates **back and forth**, and ends up where we started. **We don't travel with the wave**.
**Narrator:** That travelling disturbance is a **sound wave**. The particles stay put. It's the **energy** that travels.
**Nigel:** If the air really ran from the band to your ears, every drum solo would blow your hair off.
**Narrator:** Sound is a **longitudinal** wave: the particles vibrate in the **same direction** that the wave travels.
**Nigel:** So we bunch up, then spread out. Bunched up is a **compression**. Spread out is a **rarefaction**.
**Archie:** Oh! Oh! Is it like a stadium wave?
**Nigel:** No. In a stadium wave, people move up and down, **across** the direction of travel. That's **transverse**.
**Nigel:** **Light** is transverse. So are ripples on water. Sound is longitudinal. We go **along**.
**Narrator:** The material sound travels through is its **medium**: a **solid**, a **liquid** or a **gas**. Here, it's Nigel.
**Narrator:** Next door, the Year 8s are doing a science experiment. With a bell.
**Belle:** Hello. I'm Belle. Electric bell. I ring for the end of recess.
**Belle:** Thirty years. Nobody has ever been happy to hear me.
**Nigel:** Belle. The least popular sound in the school. Below the recorder.
**Narrator:** The **bell-jar experiment**. Belle hangs in a sealed glass jar, not touching the sides. She rings. Everyone hears her.
**Narrator:** Then a **vacuum pump** removes the air from the jar. Nigel's cousins, mostly.
**Narrator:** The ringing gets **quieter and quieter**, even though you can still **see** the hammer hitting the bell.
**Belle:** I'm still ringing! Can anyone hear me?
**Nigel:** Sound needs particles to pass it on. A **vacuum** has **no particles**. Nobody to pass it on to.
**Nigel:** But **light doesn't need a medium**. That's why they can still see her.
**Narrator:** Let the air back in, and the sound returns.
**Belle:** They're... happy to hear me? Nobody has ever been happy to hear me.
**Nigel:** Space is a vacuum too. So space is **silent**. Whatever the films say.
**Narrator:** So astronauts on spacewalks talk by **radio**. Radio waves, like light, cross a vacuum.
**Archie:** I made a rhyme! **No air, no aware**!
**Narrator:** Four p.m. A thunderstorm rolls in over the HDB blocks. Very Singapore.
**Narrator:** Kavya sees the lightning first. The thunder arrives **seconds later**.
**Nigel:** Light travels at about **300,000,000 m/s**. Sound in air? About **340 m/s**.
**Nigel:** Light is nearly a **million times** faster. We're not even in the same race.
**Narrator:** Count the seconds from flash to bang, and **divide by three**. That's roughly the storm's distance in **kilometres**.
**Kavya:** One... two... three... four... five... six.
**Archie:** Six divided by three! **Two kilometres**!
**Kavya:** Two kilometres. That's the hawker centre. Somebody's chicken rice is getting wet.
**Nigel:** Team Gas. That's us. In air, about **340 m/s**. We're the **slowest**.
**Narrator:** Team Liquid. Water. About **1,500 m/s**: more than four times faster.
**Narrator:** Team Solid. Steel. About **5,000 m/s**. The **fastest** of all.
**Archie:** But air's so light and easy to push through!
**Nigel:** Everyone thinks that. It's backwards. The **closer** packed the particles, the **faster** they pass it on. **Solids speed, gases go slow.**
**Narrator:** Every sound has a **pitch**, how high or low it is, and a **loudness**. Meet two very different colleagues.
**Freq:** Hi! I'm Freq! **Frequency**! Vibrations per second, in **hertz**! **One hertz** is **one vibration per second**!
**Amp:** I'M AMP. **AMPLITUDE**. HOW FAR THE PARTICLES MOVE FROM THEIR **REST POSITION**.
**Nigel:** Freq runs on bubble tea. Amp does not have an indoor voice.
**Freq:** **Pitch** depends on me! **High frequency**, **high pitch**, like a whistle! **Low frequency**, **low pitch**, like a bass drum!
**Amp:** **LOUDNESS** DEPENDS ON ME. **BIG AMPLITUDE**, **LOUD**. **SMALL AMPLITUDE**, **QUIET**.
**Archie:** So a high note is a loud note!
**Freq:** (whispering) Nope. High pitch. Small amplitude. High and quiet.
**Amp:** LOW PITCH. BIG AMPLITUDE. LOW AND LOUD.
**Nigel:** They're **independent**. Pitch goes with frequency, loudness goes with amplitude. **Fast pitch, big bang.**
**Freq:** Higher note on a guitar? **Tighten** the string, **shorten** it, or use a **thinner** one!
**Amp:** LOUDER? PLUCK **HARDER**. SAME NOTE.
**Narrator:** A **microphone** turns sound into an electrical signal. An **oscilloscope** draws it as a wavy line: a **trace**.
**Nigel:** **Height** shows **amplitude**: tall is **loud**. **Spacing** shows **frequency**: close together is **high-pitched**.
**Narrator:** Trace **A**: tall waves, far apart. Trace **B**: short waves, close together. Describe each sound.
**Archie:** A is **loud** and **low**! B is **quiet** and **high**!
**Nigel:** Correct. I'm as surprised as you are.
**Narrator:** One whole wave, say compression to compression, is a **wavelength**, measured in **metres**.
**Freq:** And the **time period**, **T**, is the time for one wave! **T = 1 ÷ f**! Five hertz? A fifth of a second each!
**Nigel:** The **wave equation**: **speed = frequency × wavelength**. In air, every pitch has the same speed, so **higher frequency** means **shorter wavelength**.
**Narrator:** At last, the ding reaches its customer: Kavya's **ear**.
**Coco:** Welcome to the ear. I'm Coco, the **cochlea**. Front desk, inner ear.
**Coco:** The **pinna**, the flap you can see, funnels sound into the **ear canal**.
**Coco:** The wave makes the **ear drum** vibrate: a thin, tight membrane.
**Coco:** Three tiny **bones** pass the vibrations on to me. I'm a coiled tube, full of fluid. It's a look.
**Coco:** My cells turn the vibrations into **nerve signals** for the **brain**.
**Coco:** But I only accept about **20 Hz** to **20,000 Hz**: the human **hearing range**. Twenty to twenty k. The top end drops with age.
**Freq:** Above twenty thousand hertz, I'm **ultrasound**! Below twenty, I'm **infrasound**! Elephants rumble in it!
**Narrator:** Outside that range is still real sound. A dog hears a dog whistle at about **25,000 Hz**. You hear nothing.
**Coco:** **Very loud sounds** carry lots of energy. They can damage my cells **permanently**.
**Amp:** SORRY.
**Narrator:** Hard, flat surfaces, like tiled walls, **reflect** sound. A reflected sound you hear a moment later is an **echo**.
**Echo:** ...an echo.
**Narrator:** Soft things, like curtains and carpet, **absorb** sound instead.
**Echo:** ...mmf.
**Freq:** Ultrasound echoes make **medical scans**, like a baby before it's born! Ultrasound in a liquid **cleans** jewellery too!
**Nigel:** And **sonar**. A ship sends ultrasound down into the sea, and times the echo.
**Narrator:** The echo returns after **4 seconds**. Sound in water travels at about **1,500 m/s**. How deep is the sea?
**Nigel:** That's **there and back**. Cut it in half. The sea is **3,000 metres** deep.
**Archie:** I knew that.
**Echo:** ...knew that.

chapters.title: The cast saves you some marks

lines.cap: **Narrator:** Before the credits, the cast would like to save you some marks.
**Belle:** One. Sound **cannot** travel through a vacuum. No particles. Trust me.
**Archie:** Two! Particles **don't** travel with the wave! They vibrate! The **energy** does!
**Freq:** Three! **Pitch** depends on **frequency**!
**Amp:** **LOUDNESS** DEPENDS ON **AMPLITUDE**. DON'T MIX US UP.
**Nigel:** Four. Sound is about **340 m/s**. Light is about **300,000,000 m/s**. Not similar.
**Coco:** Five. Hertz for frequency. Metres per second for speed. Units matter.
**Archie:** Six! In echo sums, the sound goes **there and back**, so cut it in half!
**Narrator:** Pass It On will return.
**Kavya:** Wait. Bar forty-seven. This is it. My moment.
**Narrator:** Ding.
**Echo:** ...ding.
**Kavya:** Nailed it.
**Echo:** ...nailed it.
